## Where This Fits
**Week 11 joined recognition, a language model and synthesis into one model, yet the largest cell of the latency budget did not move: the model still waits for an outside module to say that the user has finished.** Week 1 measured that cell at about seventy per cent of the response time, and Week 10 showed why a voice activity detector cannot fill it — it knows only whether there is sound now. **This week asks one question: the user has stopped — have they finished, or not? On what evidence is that decided, when, and where in the system?**

**We look at how people do it before we model it**, because without a reference for what counts as a good turn-taking decision no model can be evaluated. Conversation analysis and psycholinguistics give three facts, and each part of the lecture starts from one of them. First, **human turn transitions leave almost no gap**: the most common transition time is near zero, while planning even a single word takes on the order of 600 ms — so the next speaker begins preparing *before* the current one has finished, by predicting ("projecting") the end of the turn. Second, **there are two kinds of silence and they cannot be told apart at the moment they occur**: a pause inside one speaker's turn and a gap between two speakers are acoustically the same thing, and which one a silence was becomes known only when someone speaks next. Pauses inside a turn are often longer than gaps between turns. Third, **silence is the most reliable cue and the last to arrive**: in a study of Taiwan Mandarin dialogue, classifiers using either words or prosody identified the ends of turn units well when the length of the following silence was available, and much less well without it. Reliability and timeliness pull in opposite directions; that tension runs through the week.

**The first half is about the problem, the second about the decision.** First half: how people take turns (the reference); why a silence threshold is not enough — one parameter ties response speed to the rate of cutting in, and the trade-off curve obtained by sweeping it is simply the distribution of within-turn pause lengths, a property of the speaker rather than of the detector, so a better voice activity detector cannot move it; and what prediction can rest on — cues that arrive before the speaker stops, such as syntactic and pragmatic completeness, falling pitch and final lengthening, modelled from text (TurnGPT), from audio (voice activity projection), or from both (the turn detectors of 2025–2026). Second half: a prediction is a probability, and **when to act on it is a question of cost** — what one interruption and one more second of waiting are each worth depends on the application, and preparing a response can be separated from committing to it; **there is more than one decision** — while the system itself is speaking, a listener's "mm-hm", a genuine interruption and speech addressed to someone else each call for a different reaction; and **where the decision is made** — in an external module, in a predictor that reads the language model's hidden states, or in the token sequence itself, at which point nothing in the system is called a decision any more: the model emits something at every frame. The decision has not vanished; it has moved into the training data. That is the entrance to Week 13.

On the three course axes. **Representation:** what does the deciding model read — a detector's posterior, continuous acoustic features, text tokens (which require a recogniser's partial hypotheses), or both? A text-only model cannot see the pitch at the end of an utterance; an audio-only model must learn syntax on its own. The output is also a choice of representation: voice activity projection does not output "finished or not" but one of 256 patterns of who will be speaking over the next two seconds. **Latency:** we fill in the first cell of Week 1's budget. With a threshold it is a setting, not a computation time; with a predictor the wait becomes a function of confidence and can approach zero; preparing in advance moves part of the later cells to before the user has finished. Week 1's second budget — how fast the system stops when interrupted — is filled in as well. The target is not zero: human transition times form a distribution, anything earlier than zero is overlap, and delays beyond roughly 600–700 ms begin to be heard as reluctance. **Supervision:** where the labels come from — the future voice activity itself (self-supervised), speaker-change marks in transcripts, text labelled by a language model and spoken by a synthesiser, or real two-channel conversation, which is the scarcest and the only source that teaches timing.

For the local languages, three points of different strength. In **Taiwan Mandarin**, turn-final lowering is superimposed on lexical tone and remains detectable: in spontaneous dialogues, final syllables of turn units were lower in pitch and intensity than initial ones, with all tones lowered together and their relative heights largely preserved (a small study: five dialogues, one corpus). **Turn-taking models do not transfer across languages for free**, and Mandarin appears to lean on pitch more than English does: a model trained on one of English, Mandarin and Japanese degrades on the others, a jointly trained model recovers, and flattening the pitch of the input costs about two points of accuracy in Mandarin and Japanese but almost nothing in English. The frequency and timing of backchannels also differ between languages. For **Taiwanese Hokkien and Hakka** we have found no turn-taking corpus study or model; whether citation tones plus tone sandhi make the turn-final pitch cue harder to read is, for now, a prediction.

## Learning Objectives
1. Describe turn-taking in the vocabulary of conversation analysis (turn-constructional units, transition-relevance places, the turn-allocation rules); define inter-pausal units, pauses, gaps, overlaps and the signed transition time on two channels of voice activity; and explain why the fact that a silence cannot be classified as a pause or a gap at the moment it occurs is the core of the problem.
2. Derive from two quantities — the distribution of transition times and the planning time of speech production — that human speakers must predict the ends of turns; list the cues available for prediction (syntactic and pragmatic completeness, pitch, lengthening, intensity, fillers), when each becomes available, and which experiments support each.
3. Write the rule of threshold-based endpointing; show that both of its quantities (the extra wait and the probability of cutting in) are determined by the distribution of within-turn pause lengths; draw the curve obtained by sweeping the threshold; and explain why a better voice activity detector does not move that curve.
4. State the prediction targets and label sources of a text-side model (TurnGPT: the probability that the next token is a turn-shift token) and an audio-side model (voice activity projection: two seconds ahead, two speakers, eight bins, 256 classes); explain why the future pattern is modelled as one class rather than eight independent probabilities; and compare what each of these, and a combined acoustic–linguistic turn detector, cannot see.
5. Formulate "when to start speaking" as a cost problem: compute a posterior from a prior, the length of the silence so far and the pause distribution; obtain a threshold from the ratio of the cost of cutting in to the cost of waiting; distinguish preparing a response from committing to it; and argue for different cost ratios in different applications.
6. Distinguish the user behaviours that occur while the system is speaking (a backchannel, an interruption, overlap followed by continuation, speech not addressed to the system) and the reaction each calls for; write the stopping budget; and explain why the same quantity, overlap, is good in one situation and bad in another.
7. Locate where a given system makes its turn-taking decision (an external module, a predictor reading hidden states, the token sequence) and say where the decision has gone once it is written into the token sequence; define the evaluation quantities — the distribution of response latency, the take-over rate at pauses, the stopping latency — and explain why a single accuracy figure cannot compare two turn detectors.

## References
**Overviews (the backbone reading for this week)**
- Skantze, **Turn-taking in Conversational Systems and Human-Robot Interaction: A Review**, *Computer Speech & Language* 67:101178, 2021 (DOI 10.1016/j.csl.2020.101178) — from the linguistic concepts and the multimodal cues to the modelling of end-of-turn detection, interruptions and multi-party interaction; if you read one paper this week, read this one
- **JM3** Ch 26, *Conversation and its Structure* — turns, speech acts, grounding and dialogue structure in computational terms
- Levinson & Torreira, **Timing in turn-taking and its implications for processing models of language**, *Frontiers in Psychology* 6:731, 2015 (DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00731) — the argument that transition times are incompatible with the planning time of speech production, so speakers must predict
- Lu et al. (18 authors), **A Survey of Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Systems: Architectural Hierarchy, Interaction Ontology, and Decision State Machine**, arXiv:2606.19453 (2026; preprint) — the source of the four levels at which a system can make its duplex decision, and the backbone of Week 13

**How people take turns**
- Sacks, Schegloff & Jefferson, **A Simplest Systematics for the Organization of Turn-Taking for Conversation**, *Language* 50(4):696–735, 1974 (DOI 10.2307/412243) — turn-constructional units, transition-relevance places and the turn-allocation rules; where the field begins
- Duncan, **Some signals and rules for taking speaking turns in conversations**, *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* 23(2):283–292, 1972 (DOI 10.1037/h0033031) — the origin of turn-yielding cues
- Stivers et al., **Universals and Cultural Variation in Turn-Taking in Conversation**, *PNAS* 106(26):10587–10592, 2009 (DOI 10.1073/pnas.0903616106) — transition times in ten languages
- Heldner & Edlund, **Pauses, gaps and overlaps in conversations**, *Journal of Phonetics* 38(4):555–568, 2010 (DOI 10.1016/j.wocn.2010.08.002) — operational definitions of pauses, gaps and overlaps, and their distributions in conversational corpora
- Heldner, **Detection thresholds for gaps, overlaps, and no-gap-no-overlaps**, *JASA* 130(1):508–513, 2011 (DOI 10.1121/1.3598457) — gaps and overlaps become audible at about 120 ms: a reference for how precise timing needs to be
- Indefrey & Levelt, **The spatial and temporal signatures of word production components**, *Cognition* 92:101–144, 2004 (DOI 10.1016/j.cognition.2002.06.001) — the source of the 600 ms planning time
- de Ruiter, Mitterer & Enfield, **Projecting the End of a Speaker's Turn: A Cognitive Cornerstone of Conversation**, *Language* 82(3):515–535, 2006 (DOI 10.1353/lan.2006.0130) — with pitch flattened and words intact, listeners still anticipate turn ends; with pitch intact and words removed, they do much worse
- Bögels & Torreira, **Listeners use intonational phrase boundaries to project turn ends in spoken interaction**, *Journal of Phonetics* 52:46–57, 2015 (DOI 10.1016/j.wocn.2015.04.004) — the counterpart: when syntax leaves the end point open, listeners use intonational phrase boundaries
- Gravano & Hirschberg, **Turn-taking cues in task-oriented dialogue**, *Computer Speech & Language* 25(3):601–634, 2011 (DOI 10.1016/j.csl.2010.10.003) — a systematic study of turn-yielding and backchannel-inviting cues
- Roberts & Francis, **Identifying a temporal threshold of tolerance for silent gaps after requests**, *JASA* 133(6):EL471–EL477, 2013 (DOI 10.1121/1.4802900); Kendrick & Torreira, **The Timing and Construction of Preference: A Quantitative Study**, *Discourse Processes* 52(4):255–289, 2015 (DOI 10.1080/0163853X.2014.955997) — how a response that arrives late is interpreted
- Schegloff, **Overlapping talk and the organization of turn-taking for conversation**, *Language in Society* 29(1):1–63, 2000 (DOI 10.1017/S0047404500001019) — how overlaps begin and how they are resolved
- Ward & Tsukahara, **Prosodic features which cue back-channel responses in English and Japanese**, *Journal of Pragmatics* 32(8):1177–1207, 2000 (DOI 10.1016/S0378-2166(99)00109-5); Clancy, Thompson, Suzuki & Tao, **The conversational use of reactive tokens in English, Japanese, and Mandarin**, *Journal of Pragmatics* 26(3):355–387, 1996 (DOI 10.1016/0378-2166(95)00036-4) — prosodic cues for backchannels and cross-linguistic differences, including Mandarin
- For the origin of the term *backchannel* and early statistics on pauses and gaps, search *Yngve 1970 On getting a word in edgewise* and *ten Bosch Oostdijk Boves 2005 temporal aspects of turn taking*

**Thresholds, endpointing and decisions**
- Ferrer, Shriberg & Stolcke, **Is the Speaker Done Yet? Faster and More Accurate End-of-Utterance Detection Using Prosody**, ICSLP 2002, pp. 2061–2064 (DOI 10.21437/ICSLP.2002-565) — the two faults of a pause threshold, stated more than twenty years ago
- Shannon, Simko, Chang & Parada, **Improved End-of-Query Detection for Streaming Speech Recognition**, Interspeech 2017, pp. 1909–1913 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2017-496) — silence detection and end-of-query detection are different tasks; reporting latency at a given accuracy
- Chang, Prabhavalkar, He, Sainath & Simko, **Joint Endpointing and Decoding with End-to-end Models**, ICASSP 2019, pp. 5626–5630 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.2019.8683109) — folding the endpointer into an end-to-end recogniser; the link to Week 4's transducer
- Raux & Eskenazi, **A Finite-State Turn-Taking Model for Spoken Dialog Systems**, NAACL-HLT 2009 (DOI 10.3115/1620754.1620846); and **Optimizing the Turn-Taking Behavior of Task-Oriented Spoken Dialog Systems**, *ACM Transactions on Speech and Language Processing* 9(1):1–23, 2012 (DOI 10.1145/2168748.2168749) — choosing a turn-taking action at every moment from a cost matrix and decision theory
- Schlangen & Skantze, **A General, Abstract Model of Incremental Dialogue Processing**, *Dialogue & Discourse* 2(1):83–111, 2011 (DOI 10.5087/dad.2011.105); Skantze & Hjalmarsson, **Towards incremental speech generation in conversational systems**, *Computer Speech & Language* 27(1):243–262, 2013 (DOI 10.1016/j.csl.2012.05.004) — incremental processing, in which hypotheses can be revoked and commitments cannot

**Prediction from text and from audio**
- Ekstedt & Skantze, **TurnGPT: a Transformer-based Language Model for Predicting Turn-taking in Spoken Dialog**, Findings of EMNLP 2020, pp. 2981–2990 (DOI 10.18653/v1/2020.findings-emnlp.268; arXiv:2010.10874) — the text-side model
- Skantze, **Towards a General, Continuous Model of Turn-taking in Spoken Dialogue using LSTM Recurrent Neural Networks**, SIGDIAL 2017, pp. 220–230 (DOI 10.18653/v1/W17-5527) — the first continuous model of future voice activity, with independent bins
- Ekstedt & Skantze, **Voice Activity Projection: Self-supervised Learning of Turn-taking Events**, Interspeech 2022, pp. 5190–5194 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2022-10955; arXiv:2205.09812) — the main paper of the week: two seconds, eight bins, 256 classes
- Ekstedt & Skantze, **How Much Does Prosody Help Turn-taking? Investigations using Voice Activity Projection Models**, SIGDIAL 2022, pp. 541–551 (DOI 10.18653/v1/2022.sigdial-1.51; arXiv:2209.05161) — perturbation experiments on which prosodic cues the model uses
- Inoue, Jiang, Ekstedt, Kawahara & Skantze, **Real-time and Continuous Turn-taking Prediction Using Voice Activity Projection**, arXiv:2401.04868 (2024; listed on arXiv as accepted at IWSDS 2024) — real-time operation on a CPU
- Inoue, Jiang, Ekstedt, Kawahara & Skantze, **Multilingual Turn-taking Prediction Using Voice Activity Projection**, LREC-COLING 2024, pp. 11873–11883 (ACL Anthology 2024.lrec-main.1036; arXiv:2403.06487) — English, Mandarin and Japanese; limited transfer between languages; the pitch-flattening experiment
- Inoue, Lala, Skantze & Kawahara, **Yeah, Un, Oh: Continuous and Real-time Backchannel Prediction with Fine-tuning of Voice Activity Projection**, NAACL 2025, pp. 7171–7181 (DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.367; arXiv:2410.15929); Inoue et al. (8 authors), **Multilingual and Continuous Backchannel Prediction: A Cross-lingual Study**, arXiv:2512.14085 (2025; listed on arXiv as accepted at IWSDS 2026) — frame-level backchannel prediction; the second covers Chinese
- Russell, Charuau & Harte, **The Role of Prosodic and Lexical Cues in Turn-Taking with Self-Supervised Speech Representations**, ICASSP 2026, pp. 16307–16311 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP55912.2026.11464984; arXiv:2601.13835) — the model can rely on prosody or on words when the other is removed
- Wang et al. (9 authors), **Turn-taking and Backchannel Prediction with Acoustic and Large Language Model Fusion**, ICASSP 2024, pp. 12121–12125 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP48485.2024.10447196; arXiv:2401.14717) — fusing an acoustic model with a language model outperforms either alone
- Skantze & Irfan, **Applying General Turn-Taking Models to Conversational Human-Robot Interaction**, HRI 2025, pp. 859–868 (DOI 10.1109/HRI61500.2025.10973958; arXiv:2501.08946) — TurnGPT and voice activity projection deployed together on a robot, in a study with 39 participants
- Qi & Skantze, **MuVAP: Multimodal Multiparty Voice Activity Projection for Turn-taking Prediction in the wild**, Interspeech 2026, pp. 5952–5961 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2026-1381) — more than two speakers, and vision: the edge of this week's framework

**Acoustic–linguistic turn detectors (2025–2026)**
- Li et al. (11 authors), **Easy Turn: Integrating Acoustic and Linguistic Modalities for Robust Turn-Taking in Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Systems**, arXiv:2509.23938 (2025; preprint) — four turn states, open source, and a detailed account of how its training set was built
- Wu et al. (9 authors), **Phoenix-VAD: Streaming Semantic Endpoint Detection for Full-Duplex Speech Interaction**, arXiv:2509.20410 (2025; preprint)
- Wang et al. (11 authors), **FastTurn: Unifying Acoustic and Streaming Semantic Cues for Low-Latency and Robust Turn Detection**, arXiv:2604.01897 (2026; preprint) — semantic cues from streaming CTC decoding, with a test set of real human dialogue
- Pan et al. (5 authors), **JAL-Turn: Joint Acoustic-Linguistic Modeling for Real-Time and Robust Turn-Taking Detection in Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Systems**, arXiv:2603.26515 (2026; listed on arXiv as accepted at NCMMSC 2026) — shares a frozen recogniser encoder, so detection runs in parallel with recognition
- Xia et al. (5 authors), **Semantic-Aware Interruption Detection in Spoken Dialogue Systems: Benchmark, Metric, and Model**, ICME 2026 (arXiv:2603.24144) — the interruption side, with a metric that converts both kinds of error into seconds
- Three open-source tools, documented by model cards and repository READMEs rather than peer-reviewed papers: Smart Turn v3 (`pipecat-ai/smart-turn-v3`), a turn detector that reads the waveform directly; the LiveKit turn detector (`livekit/turn-detector`), which reads text only; and MaAI (`MaAI-Kyoto/MaAI`), a real-time implementation of voice activity projection

**Where the decision is made: control tokens, and how full-duplex models behave**
- Wang et al. (6 authors), **A Full-duplex Speech Dialogue Scheme Based On Large Language Models**, NeurIPS 2024 (arXiv:2405.19487) — a language model that emits control tokens to switch a two-state machine between speaking and listening
- Zhang et al. (6 authors), **LLM-Enhanced Dialogue Management for Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Systems**, arXiv:2502.14145 (2025; preprint) — a 0.5B "semantic VAD" with four control tokens
- Li & Chu, **Decoupling Turn-Taking from Semantics: A Decoupled Data Approach for Finite-State-Machine-Based Full-Duplex Dialogue**, EMNLP 2026 (arXiv:2609.03321) — synthetic text cannot teach timing; turn-taking is learned from real two-channel dialogue
- Pan et al. (9 authors), **Enabling Proactive Spoken Turns via a Generalized Style-Aware Full-Duplex Framework**, ACM MM 2026 (arXiv:2608.28630) — proactive turns and a plug-in turn controller
- Ding et al. (5 authors), **Personal VAD: Speaker-Conditioned Voice Activity Detection**, Odyssey 2020, pp. 433–439 (DOI 10.21437/Odyssey.2020-62; arXiv:1908.04284) — from "someone is speaking" to "the user is speaking"
- Arora et al. (5 authors), **Talking Turns: Benchmarking Audio Foundation Models on Turn-Taking Dynamics**, ICLR 2025 (arXiv:2503.01174) — where a full-duplex model and a detector-based cascade each go wrong
- Ohashi, Zeghidour, Défossez & Kharitonov, **Multi-Faceted Interactivity Alignment in Full-Duplex Speech Models**, EMNLP 2026 (arXiv:2606.11167) — returns in Week 14; its released samples are the recordings analysed in this week's lecture
- Lin et al. (7 authors), **Full-Duplex-Bench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Full-duplex Spoken Dialogue Models on Turn-taking Capabilities**, ASRU 2025 (arXiv:2503.04721) — pause handling, backchannelling, turn-taking and interruption; returns in Week 14
- Zhang et al. (5 authors), **TurnNat: Automatic Evaluation of Turn-Taking Naturalness in Dyadic Spoken Dialogue**, arXiv:2607.01345 (2026; preprint) — scoring the naturalness of timing with the likelihood of a predictive model
- Riera et al. (5 authors), **Synchronization and Turn-Taking in Full-Duplex Speech Dialogue Models**, arXiv:2605.20356 (2026; preprint) — anticipatory turn-taking information can be read from a full-duplex model's internal states
- Nguyen et al., **Generative Spoken Dialogue Language Modeling**, TACL 2023; Défossez et al., **Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue**, arXiv:2410.00037 — the main papers of Week 13; this week uses only their turn-taking statistics and behaviour
- Jiang et al. (6 authors), **Cocktail-Talker: Multi-Speaker Dialog Modeling in Noisy Social Environments with Turn Action GRPO**, arXiv:2607.27756 (2026; preprint) — respond, keep listening, or ignore

**Local languages**
- Levow, **Turn-taking in Mandarin Dialogue: Interactions of Tone and Intonation**, Fourth SIGHAN Workshop on Chinese Language Processing, 2005 (ACL Anthology I05-3010) — spontaneous Taiwan Mandarin dialogue: turn-final lowering of pitch and intensity with the relative heights of the tones preserved; silence as the most reliable cue
- For conversational corpora of Taiwan Mandarin and Taiwanese Hokkien, search *Taiwanese Putonghua Speech and Transcripts LDC*, *NCCU Corpus of Spoken Taiwan Mandarin*, *Taiwan Mandarin Conversational Corpus Academia Sinica*

**Further**
- Negi et al. (3 authors), **Evaluating Real-Time Voice Agents: A Survey from Component Quality to Grounded Outcomes**, arXiv:2609.30798 (2026; preprint) — turn-taking and voice activity projection from the point of view of evaluation; leads into Week 14
